meta.title: CrashFree India — State Road-Safety Governance Dataset
meta.description: Consolidated dataset merging 12 state-level road-safety governance and key-individual research files, each independently self-audited (fresh-search re-derivation + active disconfirming-evidence search) per research-rules.md. Every source citation from the original files is preserved. Every fact still flagged as UNVERIFIED / LIKELY STALE / PARTIALLY VERIFIED after the audit is carried forward here as a structured 'flag' object (badge) rather than prose, for direct rendering in a dashboard UI.

flag_resolution_category_key.a: A genuine, documented second/third attempt was made (≥2 search angles) but could not surface 2 independent corroborating sources.
flag_resolution_category_key.b: The ambiguity is genuinely unresolved in present-day reality (e.g. a contested jurisdiction, an active court stay, a transfer too recent to be reflected in any published source).

notable_corrections.summary: Deputy CM Ajit Pawar had died (28 Jan 2026) and was still listed as a serving minister — the single most significant correction across all 12 files.
The file's claim that no PWD Minister of State existed was a factual error — Brijesh Singh has held the post continuously since 2022.
The Road Construction Minister's name ("Kumar Dhirendra") did not match any source and was corrected to Kumar Shailendra; the Patna DM (who chairs the city's Road Safety Committee) had been replaced.
An active ED money-laundering investigation into the sitting PWD Minister, breaking two days before this audit, was entirely new information with direct bearing on CrashFree India's engagement plan.
Active, unresolved High Court litigation over the removal of the HYDRAA Commissioner was likewise new and directly relevant.
Resolved a standing priority question (whether the 2017 Road Safety Authority Bill was enacted) that determines which governance-model category the state belongs to.

tamil_nadu.political_context: Tamil Nadu held Legislative Assembly elections in 2026, with polling on 23 April 2026 and results on 4 May 2026. In a historic upset, the newly formed Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), led by actor C. Joseph Vijay ("Vijay"), emerged as the single largest party with 108 of 234 seats — short of a majority, producing Tamil Nadu's first hung assembly. TVK formed a coalition government with Congress and other partners' support, and Vijay was sworn in as Chief Minister on 10 May 2026, ending the DMK's M. K. Stalin government; Stalin himself lost his own seat, the first incumbent CM to lose a TN election since Jayalalithaa in 1996. Any reference to a DMK-era minister or to "Chief Minister Stalin" is now historical only. CM Vijay personally retains Home/Police, General Administration, Municipal Administration, Urban and Water Supply, and several welfare portfolios — a structural pattern similar to Bihar/Jharkhand CMs who personally hold road-safety-adjacent departments. The cabinet sworn in on 10 May 2026 assigned Public Works (Buildings, Highways and Minor Ports) and Sports Development to Aadhav Arjuna; Transport to Vijay Tamilan Parthiban (who formally assumed the portfolio on 21 May 2026, per his own biography, distinct from the 10 May general oath date); Revenue and Disaster Management to K. A. Sengottaiyan; Rural Development and Water Resources to N. Anand; Health, Medical Education and Family Welfare to Dr. K. G. Arunraj; and Housing and Urban Development to B. Rajkumar. Dr. M. Sai Kumar, IAS continues as Chief Secretary, having been granted a further six-month service extension (1 September 2026 – 28 February 2027) under Rule 16(1) of the AIS (DCRB) Rules, 1958, ahead of his original 31 August 2026 retirement date; Dr. P. Senthilkumar serves as Additional Chief Secretary/Secretary-I to the CM and G. Laxmi Priya as Secretary-II to the CM (this last detail sourced only to Elets eGov and not independently re-corroborated in this pass). (Election/succession sources: Wikipedia — 2026 Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly election, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Tamil_Nadu_Legislative_Assembly_election; Wikipedia — M. K. Stalin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._K._Stalin.)

governance_bodies.name: Tamil Nadu Road Safety Policy (2007) and State Road Safety Machinery
governance_bodies.mandate: Tamil Nadu's Road Safety Policy dates to April 2007, making it, per its own framing, the first state-level road safety policy in India, predating the National Road Safety Policy (2010). Thrust areas: Engineering, Enforcement, and Education, plus data collection, safe infrastructure, driver safety, and Emergency Medical Response. The policy itself is not a legislative Act — no specific statutory reference was found, consistent with the MV Act Section 215 executive-rules model seen in Bihar/Jharkhand rather than Karnataka's dedicated 2017 Act.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not applicable — a policy framework, not a road-owning body.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The 2007 policy proposed establishing a "lead agency" (a Road Safety Authority), but CAG's own analysis found the policy document does not detail that body's composition, chair, or meeting frequency, nor does it specify a dedicated road-safety budget/fund — a documented, independently-flagged gap in Tamil Nadu's own road-safety governance design.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs) — confirmed to exist at district level (e.g., Tirupathur district's own government portal lists a DRSC page), consistent with the national MV Act s.215(3) template, but composition, chair, and meeting frequency could not be independently fetched/confirmed in this pass (the district page itself returned a fetch error) — flagged as a priority gap.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Not established from the sources reviewed (Road Safety Authority/lead agency composition, chair, and meeting frequency not detailed in the policy itself).
governance_bodies.data_role: Data collection is named as one of the policy's thrust areas, but no dedicated statewide data mechanism is detailed in sources reviewed.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Citizen consumer and civic Action Group (CAG), a Chennai-based consumer/civic NGO (distinct from the Comptroller and Auditor General), has run District Road Safety Conferences in multiple districts (Salem, Madurai, Cuddalore) and an annual Road Safety Week press campaign, indicating an active civil-society engagement channel with DRSCs — but statewide DRSC composition and cadence remain unconfirmed.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not independently confirmed in this pass (Tirupathur DRSC page fetch blocked; no statewide DRSC roster located).

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: For CrashFree India, IIT Madras' Centre of Excellence for Road Safety / RBG Labs is Tamil Nadu's closest analogue to NIMHANS in Karnataka — a technically credible, already-active research and data partner with a working relationship to Greater Chennai Traffic Police specifically, making it a strong first technical-partnership target rather than a purely political one.
governance_bodies.data_role: RBG Labs built the crash-data dashboard underlying the national iRAD system. In January 2026, this dashboard was reported as adopted by Odisha (integrating police/officials and citizen accident-reporting portals), with plans for pan-India expansion.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The organiser.org article's TN-government-partnership framing was not itself independently corroborated with a Tamil Nadu government source in this pass (the article's confirmed content concerned Odisha's adoption) — the existence of an IIT Madras–TN government collaboration is corroborated by two other sources (careers360, Deccan Herald), but the specific current scope of that partnership was not established.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Runs recurring, dated public programmes: "Road Safety Month 2024," a "Principals' Conclave" under "Training Young Minds," a recurring "Zero Accident Day" campaign with Greater Chennai Traffic Police, and an ongoing SNS Foundation research partnership.

delhi.political_context: Delhi is not a full state but a Union Territory with a Legislative Assembly (National Capital Territory of Delhi), governed under Article 239AA of the Constitution and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991. Police, Public Order, and Land are constitutionally excluded from the Delhi government's domain and remain with the Union Government (Ministry of Home Affairs) — meaning Delhi Police does not report to the Delhi Chief Minister or any Delhi minister at all; a 2023 amendment further strengthened the Lieutenant Governor's role over "Services" (bureaucratic transfers/postings). In 2025-2026 all four apex offices changed hands: the BJP's Rekha Gupta became Chief Minister on 20 February 2025, ending a decade of AAP government under Arvind Kejriwal/Atishi; Vinai Kumar Saxena, LG since 2022, was moved to become LG of Ladakh and former diplomat Taranjit Singh Sandhu was sworn in as the new LG of Delhi on 11 March 2026 (reconfirmed still in office as of mid-April 2026); BJP's Pravesh Wahi was elected Mayor of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi on 29-30 April 2026, succeeding Raja Iqbal Singh (BJP, Apr 2025-Apr 2026) who had succeeded Mahesh Kumar Khichi (AAP, Nov 2024-Apr 2025) — the point at which mayoral control passed from AAP to BJP; and Anurag Kumar, IPS (1994-batch, AGMUT cadre), was appointed Commissioner of Delhi Police on 17 July 2026 by MHA order, replacing Satish Golcha. Practically, any Delhi engagement strategy must run on two separate, non-overlapping tracks — the elected Delhi government (PWD, Transport, MCD-adjacent civic matters) and the Union-controlled Delhi Police/MHA track — with the Lieutenant Governor sitting institutionally above both on several matters, a structure materially different from every other state in this document set.

This follows from Article 239AA of the Constitution and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991, under which Police, Public Order, and Land are constitutionally excluded from the Delhi government's domain; a 2023 amendment further strengthened the Lieutenant Governor's role over 'Services.' The Home Ministry has previously and explicitly rejected proposals to place a Traffic wing under the Delhi government.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Traffic Management Division under a Special Commissioner of Police (Traffic); DCP (Traffic) posts; DANIPS/IPS officer cadre subject to periodic MHA-ordered reshuffles.

madhya_pradesh.political_context: Dr. Mohan Yadav (BJP) has served as Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh since 13 December 2023, with Rajendra Shukla and Jagdish Devda as Deputy Chief Ministers (Wikipedia — Mohan Yadav: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohan_Yadav). The cabinet was sworn in and portfolios allocated on 25/30 December 2023, and a fresh 11 September 2026 re-audit independently re-confirmed all six road-safety-relevant portfolios directly against each minister's own Wikipedia biography, finding them unchanged apart from one narrow, dated exception: on 16 July 2026 the Animal Husbandry and Dairy Development portfolio was withdrawn from Minister of State Lakhan Patel and placed directly under the Chief Minister in a late-night notification (Goemkarponn, 16 July 2026: https://goemkarponn.com/late-night-portfolio-change-sparks-buzz-over-cabinet-reshuffle-in-madhya-pradesh/); that reshuffle does not touch any of the six road-safety-relevant portfolios. Separately, a Dainik Jagran (Madhya Pradesh) report circulating in 2026 discusses speculation about a larger cabinet reshuffle — triggered by Urban Development Minister Kailash Vijayvargiya's political standing after the Dec 2025-Jan 2026 Bhagirathpura (Indore) contaminated-water tragedy — naming Vijayvargiya, Prahlad Singh Patel, Dilip Ahirwar, and Radha Singh as ministers who "could" see portfolios changed, while explicitly stating "no official confirmation has come from the CM's office" and floating a possible window no earlier than mid-2026 (Dainik Jagran English: https://english.dainikjagranmpcg.com/states/madhya-pradesh/seo-headline-mp-cabinet-reshuffle-2026-mohan-yadav-eyes-ministry/article-15391). As of the research date (11 September 2026) no such reshuffle has occurred and both ministers' Wikipedia pages still show their December 2023 portfolios, but Vijayvargiya's and Patel's portfolios should be treated as most at near-term risk of change and reconfirmed before any high-stakes outreach. CM Mohan Yadav personally retains General Administration, Home, Jail, and Industrial Policy and Investment Promotion, meaning — as in Bihar, Jharkhand, and Tamil Nadu — the Chief Minister personally controls the police/enforcement chain, a recurring structural pattern across states in this document set. The DGP is Kailash Makwana, IPS (1988-batch), appointed 1 December 2024 by Home Department order dated 23 November 2024, originally due to retire December 2025 but extended to December 2026 under Supreme Court two-year-minimum-tenure guidelines; a fresh 11 September 2026 re-check found no replacement, resignation, or transfer, so his tenure through December 2026 stands reconfirmed.

assam.political_context: Assam held Legislative Assembly elections in 2026, and Himanta Biswa Sarma (BJP) was returned for a second term as Chief Minister, with the new (Second Sarma) ministry sworn in on 12 May 2026 in an initial CM-plus-four ceremony, followed by a full cabinet expansion of 12 additional ministers on 5 June 2026, bringing the council of ministers to 17 (14 BJP, 2 AGP, 1 BPF). CM Himanta Biswa Sarma personally holds an unusually concentrated set of portfolios: Home (except Prisons, Home Guards), Personnel, Public Works (Buildings & National Highways), Public Works (Roads), and Medical Education & Research -- described in the source research as the most concentrated portfolio structure found across all states researched in that series, since it gives one office simultaneous control of enforcement (Home/Police), road engineering (both PWD wings), and medical education (relevant to trauma-care training). Other cabinet portfolios relevant to road safety are Transport & Welfare of Bodoland (Charan Boro, BPF), Health & Family Welfare (Ashok Singhal, BJP), Revenue & Disaster Management (Keshab Mahanta, AGP), Panchayat & Rural Development / Implementation of Assam Accord / Excise / Border Protection & Development (Atul Bora, AGP), and Housing & Urban Affairs (Kaushik Rai, BJP); all five were re-verified in the 11 September 2026 pass against at least one non-Wikipedia source. Harmeet Singh, IPS (1992-batch, Assam-Meghalaya cadre) is DGP, having taken charge as acting DGP on 29 January 2025 and being formally promoted/confirmed effective 29 May 2025, after earlier serving as Guwahati Police Commissioner; he was actively re-checked for a 2026 transfer or successor and none was found, with directory snapshots dated 6 January 2026 and 16 March 2026 and a September 2026 press-meet report all consistent with him still holding the post. Assam's current district count is 35, re-checked in the verification pass and corroborated by multiple current (2026-dated) sources (Verified, Moderate Confidence, since no single authoritative Revenue Department gazette listing was checked directly). Courts relevant to road safety are Motor Accident Claims Tribunals (MACTs) for compensation and Judicial Magistrate courts for prosecutable offences; a search for a current (2025/2026) Gauhati High Court PIL specifically on road/bridge safety did not surface one -- the only identified case, a dismissal of a PIL over Maligaon Flyover construction safety, dates to 16 September 2023 and is now stale.

haryana.political_context: Nayab Singh Saini (BJP) has served as Chief Minister of Haryana since March 2024 and was returned to office after the October 2024 Haryana Legislative Assembly election, with cabinet portfolios allocated on 21 October 2024. CM Saini personally holds 12 portfolios, including Home, Finance, Planning, Excise & Taxation, Town & Country Planning, Urban Estates, Housing, Criminal Investigation, and Law & Legislative — a centralisation pattern similar to several other states in this research series (CM personally holding Home plus land-use/urban portfolios), though PWD and Transport sit with separate ministers here, unlike Assam. The full October 2024 cabinet portfolio list was independently cross-checked against a full Wikipedia cabinet-list page (Second Saini ministry) plus individual minister pages, and no reshuffle since October 2024 was found across three independent search/fetch angles. On policing, Ajay Singhal, IPS (1992-batch), took charge as Haryana DGP on 1 January 2026, with a guaranteed minimum two-year tenure under the 2006 Prakash Singh Supreme Court judgment and a natural retirement date of 31 October 2028; he succeeded O. P. Singh, who had held interim charge after predecessor Shatrujeet Singh Kapur went on leave while named as an accused in an IPS officer's suicide case. Re-verification on 11 September 2026 against the most recent Haryana IPS reshuffle (26 June 2026) confirmed Singhal remains DGP, having received only an additional charge as Chairman/MD of the Haryana Police Housing Corporation.

telangana.political_context: A. Revanth Reddy (Congress) has served as Chief Minister of Telangana since 7 December 2023, heading the state's first Congress government since Telangana's 2014 creation. Cabinet portfolios were allocated shortly after, with the CM personally retaining Municipal Administration & Urban Development (MAUD), General Administration, and Law & Order (i.e., Home/Police), plus all unallocated portfolios — meaning the same office controls both statewide enforcement and Hyderabad's urban civic administration (GHMC oversight sits under MAUD), a pattern also seen in Bihar, Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu, Assam, and Haryana. The full December 2023 cabinet portfolio list rests primarily on a single South First article, with Komatireddy Venkat Reddy (Roads and Buildings), Ponnam Prabhakar (Transport), and N. Uttam Kumar Reddy (Irrigation and CAD, Food and Civil Supplies — confirmed NOT Home Minister despite an initially ambiguous source reference) independently cross-checked against Wikipedia. C. V. Anand, IPS, took charge as Telangana DGP on 1 May 2026 and, notably for CrashFree India, immediately announced plans for a dedicated Traffic Management and Road Safety Bureau (TG-TMARS) for consistent statewide enforcement; as of the most recent source found (27 August 2026), TG-TMARS remains not operational, with Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju still directing officials to build a common traffic-data platform roughly four months after the announcement. Anand previously served as Hyderabad Police Commissioner (2024-2025), succeeded in that role by V. C. Sajjanar, IPS, who assumed charge 30 September 2025 and remains Hyderabad Police Commissioner as of this audit (September 2026), with no reports of a subsequent transfer found.

maharashtra.political_context: Maharashtra is governed by the Mahayuti coalition (BJP + Shiv Sena-Shinde + NCP-Ajit Pawar faction, the last now led by Sunetra Pawar following Ajit Pawar's death in January 2026), formed after the November 2024 state assembly election. Devendra Fadnavis (BJP) became Chief Minister for a third time on 5 December 2024 and personally holds Home Affairs, Finance, Planning, Energy, Law & Judiciary, General Administration, and Information & Public Relations -- Home gives him direct control of the state police (and therefore Highway Police oversight), consistent with the pattern seen in other states of the CM personally retaining Home. Deputy CM Eknath Shinde (Shiv Sena) holds Urban Development, Housing, and Public Works (including Public Undertakings), and is ex officio Chairman of both the MMRDA Authority and MSRDC by virtue of the Urban Development portfolio. Deputy CM Ajit Pawar (NCP), who had held Finance, Planning, and State Excise among other portfolios, died on 28 January 2026 in an air-charter crash near Baramati Airport along with four others on board; Finance and Planning passed directly to CM Fadnavis on the day of his death, and his widow Sunetra Pawar succeeded him as Deputy CM three days later (31 January 2026), retaining State Excise, Sports & Youth Welfare, and Minority Development and Aukaf, but not Finance or Planning. PWD itself is split between a 'Public Works (excluding Public Undertakings)' wing held by a dedicated PWD minister (Shivendrasinhraje Bhosale) and a 'Public Works (including Public Undertakings)' wing nominally under Shinde -- a jurisdictional split distinctive to Maharashtra among the states researched so far. The Chief Secretary is Rajesh Aggarwal, appointed 1 December 2025.

governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: 22-member body: Transport Commissioner (member-secretary), PWD and Transport ministers, state officials from Home/Transport/BMC, plus 8 special invitees (public health, urban development, media). Biannual meetings are mandatory by regulation. STANDOUT FINDING -- RECONFIRMED AND UPDATED this pass (11 Sept 2026): the Council has still not met since 4 April 2023. A newer, independent source (newsdrum.in, published 14 June 2026) directly reconfirms the gap and updates the figure: "more than 38 months have passed without a single meeting," and quotes Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik promising the Council would finally convene "in the first week of July [2026]," contingent on completion of a three-year road safety plan. A second search attempt (for evidence the promised July 2026 meeting actually occurred) found no confirming report either way. Since inception in 2015, meetings should have occurred biannually under the mandatory schedule; only 12 were actually held per the original report. A retired RTO official is quoted characterizing the gap as "administrative apathy"; officials cited election code-of-conduct restrictions, though other government committees continued meeting during the same period. Experts quoted warn that without regular review, Maharashtra cannot meet its 50% road-fatality-reduction target by 2030. The state recorded 36,567 fatalities and 83,820 accidents between January 2023 and April 2025. Separately, a Maharashtra Transport Commissioner circular (11 Feb 2026) declared 2026 the "Save Two-Wheeler Riders & Pedestrians Year" following a state-level road-safety review meeting held 28-29 January 2026 -- but this departmental review meeting is distinct from, and does not substitute for, a statutory State Road Safety Council meeting, and no source ties it to the Council specifically. This remains the single most concrete documented road-safety-governance failure found across all nine states researched to date, and if anything is more acute than originally documented (38 months and counting, not "nearly two years").

gujarat.political_context: Bhupendra Patel (BJP) has been Chief Minister of Gujarat since 13 September 2021, re-elected for a second term on 12 December 2022. Unusually compared to other states researched, CM Patel personally holds the roads-engineering portfolio himself — General Administration, Administrative Reforms & Training, Planning, and Roads and Buildings and Capital Projects — publicly announcing large project allocations under his own name (e.g., ₹7,737 crore for 124 projects, October 2025) rather than delegating roads/PWD to a separate minister. Deputy CM Harsh Sanghavi (BJP), Deputy CM since 17 October 2025, holds Home Affairs, Law and Justice, Tourism, Industries, MSME & Civil Aviation, plus (continuing from his earlier appointment of 16 September 2021) Transport, Sports/Youth Affairs/Cultural Activities, Excise & Prohibition, and Border Security & Prisons — uniquely combining Home (police) and Transport, the two levers most directly relevant to enforcement and vehicle regulation, in one office. Other road-relevant ministers include Kanubhai Desai (Finance, Urban Development, Urban Housing) and Kunvarjibhai Bavaliya (Labour, Skill Development & Employment, Rural Development). Chief Secretary Manoj Kumar Das (1990-batch IAS) took charge effective 31 October 2025, succeeding Pankaj Joshi on his superannuation, with a tenure slated through December 2026. A historical note: Jaydrathsinh Parmar held a State Minister of Roads and Buildings role from 2012–2017, and a separate Agriculture/Panchayat/Environment portfolio Dec 2017–Sept 2021, but does not currently hold any R&B portfolio.

governance_bodies.name: Gujarat Road Safety Authority (GRSA)
governance_bodies.mandate: A dedicated statutory Authority — the most institutionally developed road-safety-specific body found across all nine states researched to date alongside Karnataka's KSRSA. Established under the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018, operating under the Gujarat Road Safety Rules and Orders, 2020. Implements road safety across four pillars: enforcement, road engineering, emergency care, and education.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body — a coordinating/implementing safety authority operating across road types.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chief Road Safety Commissioner at the operational head — per Section 3(4) of the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018, this statutory post is "the Chief Executive Officer of the Authority" and "head of the staff of the Authority" — supported by a Joint Commissioner and Chief Enforcement Officer. The Authority itself has 14 statutory members drawn from Transport, Home, Health, Education, R&B, law enforcement, transport corporations, municipal administration, highway authorities, automobile associations, and two nominated road-safety experts. An Executive Committee, chaired by the Additional Chief Secretary (Transport), meets bimonthly. The broader Authority and a State Road Safety Council operate under the chairmanship of the Transport Minister (currently Deputy CM Harsh Sanghavi, by virtue of his Transport portfolio), meeting biannually. Re-verified 11 Sept 2026: statutory title corrected from "Road Safety Commissioner" to "Chief Road Safety Commissioner" per the Act text itself, upgrading the earlier single-secondary-source characterization.

uttar_pradesh.political_context: Yogi Adityanath (BJP) has been Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh since 19 March 2017, now in his second term following the 2022 election. His personal portfolio concentration is the single most extensive found across all ten states researched to date: he directly controls more than 25 departments — per one detailed account, over 36 ministries — including Home, Public Works Department (PWD), Law, Information, and Revenue. Home and PWD are explicitly described as "the two most powerful ministries in Uttar Pradesh," both retained personally by the CM (Verified, Moderate-High Confidence for the Home+PWD combination, corroborated by two independent sources though the exact department count differs, 25+ vs. ~36, between them). PWD's Cabinet-rank charge history: Keshav Prasad Maurya (now Deputy CM) held it 19 March 2017 – 25 March 2022, succeeded by Cabinet Minister Jitin Prasada (25 March 2022 – 11 June 2024), who resigned on becoming a Union Minister of State on 10 June 2024; no Cabinet-rank successor has since been appointed. A correction made in the 11 September 2026 re-verification pass establishes that a named PWD Minister of State, Brijesh Singh (BJP MLA, Deoband), has held that role continuously since 25 March 2022 and remains incumbent — running alongside Cabinet Minister Jitin Prasada until 2024 and, since Prasada's exit, without a Cabinet-rank counterpart. The CM's "direct personal control" of PWD is therefore best read as the CM retaining the vacant Cabinet-rank charge/ultimate authority, with day-to-day ministerial representation handled by MoS Brijesh Singh, rather than PWD having no minister of any rank. The two Deputy CMs are Keshav Prasad Maurya (Rural Development since 25 March 2022; Food Processing Industries since 19 March 2017) and Brajesh Pathak (Health & Family Welfare, Medical Education, Maternity & Child Welfare, since 25 March 2022). The Transport Minister is Daya Shankar Singh, Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Transport since 25 March 2022. Chief Secretary Shashi Prakash Goyal (1989-batch IAS, UP cadre) took charge on 1 August 2025, succeeding Manoj Kumar Singh (who retired 31 July 2025), and is slated to serve until his own retirement in January 2027; he was reconfirmed still serving as of the 11 September 2026 re-verification with no successor identified.

bihar.political_context: Bihar held Legislative Assembly elections in November 2025, and the state's government changed hands in April–May 2026: Nitish Kumar's uninterrupted run as Chief Minister ended on 15 April 2026, and Samrat Choudhary (BJP) was sworn in as the 24th Chief Minister the same day, with the full cabinet reshuffled and portfolios allocated on 7–8 May 2026. As of the most recent verification (9 September 2026), Samrat Choudhary was confirmed still actively functioning as CM through contemporaneous press coverage of his public appearances (felicitating students, attending public events). Under the 8 May 2026 portfolio allocation, the CM retains Home, General Administration, Vigilance, Election, Civil Aviation and unallocated departments; Deputy CM Vijay Kumar Chaudhary holds Water Resources & Parliamentary Affairs; Deputy CM Bijendra Prasad Yadav holds Finance & Commercial Taxes; Road Construction went to Kumar Shailendra; and Energy went to Shailesh Kumar ("Bulo Mandal"). This is a structural change with direct road-safety consequences: the Transport Minister (now Damodar Rawat), the Road Construction Minister (now Kumar Shailendra), and both Deputy Chief Ministers are all different people than a year ago, meaning most of Bihar's road-safety-relevant political leadership is newly in role and has, by definition, no track record yet in its current position. Underlying this political layer, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police all sit substantially on the State List (with the Union retaining National Highways, the overarching Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes like PMGSY), Bihar's state government and its departments are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue — the Union government matters mainly for NH stretches, PMGSY funding rules, and the national legal framework.

governance_bodies.name: Transport Department, Government of Bihar
governance_bodies.mandate: A Regulatory Department responsible for implementation and enforcement of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Central Motor Vehicle Rules 1989, other rules made thereunder, and State Taxation Acts, to regulate road transport, passenger and freight movement.

governance_bodies.name: Rural Works Department (RWD)
governance_bodies.mandate: Responsible for construction of rural roads with necessary culverts and cross-drainage structures.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Other District Roads (ODR) and Village Roads (VR), with the objective of improving "Farm to Market Connectivity"; implements PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme) and state-funded equivalents — Mukhya Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (MMGSY, launched 2013–14), MMGSY (Remaining) (launched 2023), and the Gramin Tola Sampark Nischay Yojana.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Structure parallel to RCD: Engineer-in-Chief (RWD), Chief Engineers, Superintending Engineers, Executive Engineers at Circle/Division level. RWD's internal Wing/Circle organisational structure was not found in as much organogram detail as RCD's (a carried-over gap).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Not always executed by RWD's own engineering staff — in the initial 2000s ramp-up, the Government of Bihar asked the Ministry of Rural Development to engage central agencies, and tripartite agreements were signed with IRCON International, National Buildings Construction Corporation, National Hydroelectric Power Corporation and National Projects Construction Corporation, along with CPWD, covering 33 of Bihar's 37 districts at the time.

governance_bodies.data_role: Acts as the road-owning-agency stakeholder in iRAD for ODR/VR crash-site design review.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: PMGSY has a three-tier quality monitoring system — internal QC by contractors at the project level, a second tier of independent State Quality Monitors inspecting in three stages, and a third tier of National Quality Monitors carrying out random field inspections and grading execution quality.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Progress of PMGSY is reviewed through Regional Review Meetings, Performance Review Committee meetings, and Empowered Committee meetings with states, plus Bihar's own internal reviews. RWD's 2025–26 budget of ₹11,101.64 crore was presented to the Assembly, reporting 764 km of MMGSY roads built in 2024–25 and a target of a further 8,600 km in 2025–26, alongside 700 new rural bridges planned for the year.

governance_bodies.name: Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural local self-government under the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 2006, implementing the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Very limited — Gram Panchayats can maintain purely internal village streets/drains where GP funds (15th Finance Commission grants, MGNREGA convergence, own tax revenue) allow; cannot independently execute PMGSY/MMGSY-scale road construction.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (GP) at village level, Panchayat Samiti at Block level, and Zila Parishad at District level — at present 8,053 Gram Panchayats, 533 Panchayat Samitis and 38 Zila Parishads are functional, with Gram Panchayats divided into roughly 1.15 lakh wards. A Gram Kachahry (village-level dispute-resolution body) exists at each GP; a Ward Sabha exists at each ward under the Ward Member, alongside the Gram Sabha at GP level.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Elected political heads: Mukhiya (GP), Pramukh (Panchayat Samiti), Adhyaksha (Zila Parishad). Administrative/executive counterparts: Panchayat Secretary (GP), BDO-cum-Executive Officer (Panchayat Samiti), and Deputy Development Commissioner-cum-CEO (Zila Parishad) — reporting up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department → Director → district BDO/DDC cadre), not to the elected head.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: A Gram Panchayat may impose a yearly tax on occupants of holdings, and on professions, trades, callings and employment carried on within its jurisdiction, subject to State Government approval of the maximum tax rate (Section 27, BPRA 2006); the State Government retains rule-making power (Section 146) and the power to issue model regulations and inquire into Panchayat affairs (Sections 150 and 152). Every Gram Panchayat must prepare a development plan annually and submit it to the Panchayat Samiti (Sections 166–167).
governance_bodies.data_role: PRIs have a formally recognised awareness/participation role in road safety — the 2020 amendment to Bihar's Road Safety Council Rules explicitly tasks the Transport Department's coordination committee with ensuring "active participation of Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies and NGOs in road safety awareness programmes" — distinct from an engineering role.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The state government intimated in Feb. 2005, based on department resolutions from September 2001, that functions of 20 departments had been devolved to PRIs — but a CAG review found that while activity mapping had been done, actual transfer of functions, functionaries and funds to PRIs by these departments had not fully materialised — a documented, audited gap between paper devolution and real administrative control.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Annual development-plan submission cycle (Sections 166–167, BPRA 2006); Gram Sabha/Ward Sabha meetings for local matters.

subordinates_parsed.text: Elected political heads: Mukhiya (GP), Pramukh (Panchayat Samiti), Adhyaksha (Zila Parishad). Administrative/executive counterparts: Panchayat Secretary (GP), BDO-cum-Executive Officer (Panchayat Samiti), and Deputy Development Commissioner-cum-CEO (Zila Parishad) — reporting up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department → Director → district BDO/DDC cadre), not to the elected head.

governance_bodies.name: Home Department / Bihar Police (incl. Traffic Police)
governance_bodies.mandate: Overall command of law and order and traffic enforcement statewide, under the Home Department (headed politically by the Chief Minister, who traditionally also holds the Home portfolio in Bihar).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — an enforcement body, not a road-owning one. Enforcement decisions (checkpoint locations, helmet/seatbelt drives, drunk-driving campaigns) are made at ADG (Traffic) and district SP level; infrastructure decisions that police influence but don't own (camera placement, signal timing, physical traffic-calming) require joint sign-off with the Transport Department and/or the road-owning engineering department.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Director General of Police (DGP) heads Bihar Police. An Additional Director General of Police (ADG), Traffic heads traffic policing statewide; district-level traffic enforcement is typically headed by an SP (Traffic) in major cities (e.g., Patna) or handled by the general district SP/SSP elsewhere, with Traffic DSPs and Traffic Inspectors/Sub-Inspectors at the operational level. Bihar has 43 Police Districts (headed by SP/SSP) and 853 Police Stations; a Police District is divided into Police Subdivisions headed by a DSP. Patna and other large cities have designated City SPs (e.g., SP City East/West) separate from rural SPs, plus a dedicated SP (Traffic), Patna.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Crime Investigation Department (CID) for serious/fatal hit-and-run or negligence cases; Economic Offences Unit; Bihar Police Academy and Constable Training School/Military Police training centres.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development & Housing Department (UDHD) and Urban Local Bodies
governance_bodies.mandate: UDHD sets urban policy; its principal implementing arm for infrastructure is BUIDCO (Bihar Urban Infrastructure Development Corporation), established 2009 under the Companies Act 1956, functioning as the apex body for planning, coordination and implementation of urban development projects (water supply, sewerage, urban transport, housing, solid waste management).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within Urban Local Body limits (Nagar Nigams/Municipal Corporations, Nagar Parishads/Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats) under the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 — as of April 2026 there were 264 Urban Local Bodies in the state. Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC, established 1952) handles municipal roads, drains, streetlights within Patna.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Each ULB has an elected wing (Mayor for Corporations, Chairperson for Councils, President for Nagar Panchayats, plus ward councillors) and a separate administrative wing; day-to-day execution runs through a Municipal Commissioner (Corporations) or Executive Officer (Councils/Nagar Panchayats), state cadre officers not directly under the elected Mayor's control for personnel matters.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: BUIDCO; the Patna Metropolitan Area Authority (PMAA) — the current metropolitan planning body, constituted under the Bihar Urban Planning & Development Act, 2012, as successor to the defunct Patna Regional Development Authority (PRDA, established 1979, dissolved 2007 when the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 repealed its enabling legislation).

governance_bodies.performance_issues: The existence of a dated 2020 amendment notification, ongoing Road Safety Week observances, and school-curriculum integration (road safety chapters for classes VI–VIII from 2014–15) indicate the Council/Lead Agency structure is at least intermittently active; no direct evidence of a regular meeting cadence was found.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified precisely; Road Safety Week is observed annually.

key_individuals.name: Shrawan Kumar
key_individuals.role: Cabinet Minister, Rural Development & Information/Public Relations (since 7 May 2026); previously Bihar's Transport Minister (28 Jan 2024 – 14 Apr 2026). [Political category: ruling party (JD(U)) leadership; former Transport administration lead]
key_individuals.priority: Moderate priority (no longer holds Transport, but retains cabinet rank, JD(U) legislature-party leadership, and a genuine track record)

track_record.text: Addressing a national conference of transport ministers in Delhi, he disclosed Bihar held 484 district-level road-safety review meetings through 2025 (involving DMs, SPs, transport and road-construction officials), ran a month-long January awareness campaign on helmets and seatbelts, and reported black-spot rectification cutting NHAI-flagged black spots from 160 (2022) to 114 (2024). He also referenced a ₹25,000 Good Samaritan reward and efforts to link private ambulances to the 102 emergency service for faster "golden hour" response.

Ordered seizure of vehicles left parked on highways for two or more days, with licence suspension for repeat offenders, explicitly framed as an accident-reduction measure (citing ~32 accidents/day statewide in 2024).

Ordered a statewide ban and enforcement drive against "jugaad" vehicles (improvised diesel-pump/motorcycle-handlebar contraptions) on state and national highways, acting on a Patna High Court order that followed a Supreme Court direction.

key_individuals.frequency_of_engagement: Recurring — at least three distinct, months-apart road-safety interventions as Transport Minister over 2025–26, plus an explicit multi-department review structure (484 meetings) that predates any single campaign.
key_individuals.background: MLA from Nalanda since 1995; JD(U); Leader of the JD(U) Legislature Party since 20 April 2026. Long-serving chief whip of JD(U) in the Bihar Assembly for years before his 2024–26 ministerial stint; political career traces to the JP Movement. Holds no specific transport/engineering background — his interventions read as enforcement- and administration-driven rather than technocratic.
key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Political access and credibility within JD(U); institutional memory of what worked (and what stalled) in the 2024–26 road-safety push; potential to champion CrashFree India's asks even from outside the Transport portfolio via his cabinet and party-leadership standing.
key_individuals.suggested_approach: Reference the specific 2025–26 initiatives (zero-fatality districts, Good Samaritan incentive, black-spot data) before proposing where CrashFree India could plug a gap (data quality, NGO capacity per the state's own Road Safety Council rules, or sustaining momentum on the districts he named).
key_individuals.caveats: Because he no longer holds the Transport portfolio, his current formal authority over road safety is limited; his value is as an informed champion and possible bridge to the current Transport Minister (Damodar Rawat) and Transport Commissioner, not as an implementer in his own right.

key_individuals.background: Born in Rohtas district, Bihar (1977). Rose to national prominence as a political strategist for Narendra Modi's 2014 campaign, then worked for the Congress, JD(U), TMC (Mamata Banerjee), DMK and AAP at various points. Briefly joined JD(U) as national vice-president in 2018 at Nitish Kumar's invitation, then was expelled in 2020 after publicly opposing the CAA/NRC. Launched the "Jan Suraaj" padyatra (foot march) across Bihar in 2022, converting it into a registered party in October 2024. His relationship with the state's police and administration has been openly adversarial — he was detained by Patna police in January 2025 during a protest over alleged BPSC exam irregularities, and has repeatedly criticized law-and-order and administrative failures under both the previous and current governments. Jan Suraaj contested all 243 seats in the November 2025 general election and failed to win a single one, prompting the party to dissolve its entire organisational structure. Kishor then won the Bankipur by-election himself in August 2026 with roughly 63,000+ votes, defeating the BJP candidate — his first-ever personal electoral victory after 15+ years as a strategist for other people's campaigns. He is brand new to elected office (about five weeks in as of the by-election). His professional background is public health, not politics — he holds a Master's in Healthcare Management (a joint program with Johns Hopkins University and Hinduja Hospital) and worked for eight years on a UN-funded public health programme before entering political strategy.
key_individuals.value_to_crashfree: Media amplification (he draws national press coverage disproportionate to a single-seat party); a genuinely relevant technical/professional lens (public health) to frame road safety around; a fresh, still-forming political voice in Patna specifically, at a moment when he has both incentive and bandwidth to build a substantive local profile as MLA.
key_individuals.suggested_approach: Lead with mortality/public-health data (his professional training) and Patna's specific, official "high-crash district" status, and consider whether his general adversarial stance toward the administration could make him receptive to positioning CrashFree India's work as independent civil-society oversight rather than government partnership. Requires intermediary, but he is unusually reachable by Indian political-leader standards — very active on social media and with journalists, given his career as a strategist.
key_individuals.caveats: That "roads and sanitation can wait" comment is worth taking seriously before any pitch — it suggests a generic "infrastructure investment" framing may land poorly with him, whereas a framing anchored in public health and preventable deaths (his actual professional background) is much more likely to resonate; this is an inference from his stated priorities, not documented interest. His single, single-seat legislative position gives him real visibility but very limited direct institutional power over Transport or Road Construction departments (both controlled by the ruling coalition) — his value is advocacy and visibility, not implementation authority, complementary to (not a substitute for) the department-level relationships already in the database.

karnataka.political_context: Siddaramaiah resigned as Chief Minister on 28 May 2026 and D. K. Shivakumar was sworn in as the 18th Chief Minister of Karnataka on 3 June 2026, with G. Parameshwara as Deputy CM, under an internal Congress power-sharing arrangement. Portfolios were allocated on 4 June 2026 and reshuffled again on 27 August 2026 when the cabinet was expanded. As of Shivakumar's 100th day in office (10-11 September 2026) he remains Chief Minister with no rotation back to Siddaramaiah having occurred, though persistent speculation about a power-sharing 'rotation' understanding means this should be re-checked before any future use of this document. Priyank Kharge became Home Minister (excluding Intelligence, which the CM retains) from the June 2026 reshuffle; Byrathi Suresh became Transport Minister, succeeding Ramalinga Reddy (who moved to Major and Medium Irrigation, then to Forest, Ecology and Environment on 13 August 2026); and Satish Jarkiholi retained Public Works through the August 2026 reshuffle. The single most significant new development is that, on 9 September 2026 — two days before this audit — the Enforcement Directorate conducted money-laundering raids at roughly 18 locations linked to PWD Minister Satish Jarkiholi, including his Bengaluru residence and properties tied to his daughter, MP Priyanka Jarkiholi, and other relatives/associates; as of the most recent reporting located (10 September 2026) he remains PWD Minister with no resignation or removal reported, but this is an active, fast-moving situation that could affect the stability of the PWD ministerial relationship on short notice. Any reference to 'Transport Minister Ramalinga Reddy' or 'CM Siddaramaiah' is now historically relevant only, not a current contact.

governance_bodies.name: Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) and the five City Corporations
governance_bodies.mandate: Greater Bengaluru Governance Act, 2024 (Karnataka Act No. 36 of 2025) abolished the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) and the BBMP Act, 2020, effective 15 May 2025, and replaced them with a three-tier structure: GBA at the apex (chaired by the Chief Minister); five City Corporations (Bengaluru Central, North, South, East and West); and Ward Committees below that. Fully operationalised from 2 September 2025.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Each of the five City Corporations is the formal owner/custodian of municipal roads, footpaths, drains and streetlights within its zone, exactly as BBMP was before it.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: GBA (chaired by CM Shivakumar, bringing together all state ministers, Bengaluru-area MPs/MLAs/MLCs, and once elected, the five corporations' Mayors) -> Five City Corporations, each headed (in the absence of an elected Mayor) by an appointed IAS Municipal Commissioner -> Ward Committees. Bengaluru's roughly 198 former BBMP wards were redrawn and expanded into 369 wards across the five corporations (63 Central, 72 North, 72 South, 50 East, 112 West).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Parastatal bodies coordinated under the GBA umbrella: BESCOM (electricity), BWSSB (water/sewerage), BMTC (city bus transport), BMRCL (metro rail); also Bengaluru Solid Waste Management Ltd.

jharkhand.political_context: Hemant Soren (Jharkhand Mukti Morcha, JMM) has led an INDIA-bloc coalition government (JMM + Congress + RJD) continuously since re-election in December 2024, following the JMM-led alliance's 56/81-seat win in the November 2024 Assembly election; he has served as Chief Minister since 4 July 2024 (having previously held the post 2019-2024 and briefly in 2013-2014) and as President of the JMM since 15 April 2025. This was reconfirmed current via the Jharkhand Transport Department's live official website during this verification pass (Hemant Soren — Wikipedia; Transport Department, Government of Jharkhand — live site). The cabinet sworn in with him has been largely stable since December 2024, with three significant recent disruptions: the Director General of Police post has changed hands three times in under two years (Anurag Gupta → Tadasha Mishra, acting → Tadasha Mishra, regular, the last change in late December 2025); Cabinet Minister Sudivya Kumar (JMM, Urban Development & Housing, Higher/Technical Education, Tourism, Sports & Youth Affairs) died of cardiac arrest on 6 September 2026 in Giridih, five days before this corrected pass, leaving the Urban Development & Housing portfolio vacant with no successor announced as of 11 September 2026; and Ranchi's Deputy Commissioner has changed from Manjunath Bhajantri to Varun Ranjan, IAS, per the official Ranchi district government website (ranchi.nic.in), confirming a currentness risk the original document had itself flagged (a May 2025 20-district DC reshuffle). Structurally, Chief Minister Hemant Soren personally holds Home, Personnel, Administrative Reforms, Road Construction, Building Construction, and all unallocated departments, while Transport sits with a separate cabinet minister (JMM's Deepak Birua, who also holds Revenue and Registration & Land Reforms) — meaning road engineering decisions (black-spot correction, highway design standards) run through the CM's own department rather than a separate Road Construction Minister. Congress's Radhakrishna Kishore holds Finance, Commercial Tax, Planning and Development, and Parliamentary Affairs; RJD's Sanjay Prasad Yadav holds Industries, Labour, Planning, and Training and Skill Development; Congress's Irfan Ansari holds Health, Medical Education and Family Welfare, plus Food, Public Distribution, and Consumer Affairs; and Dipika/Deepika Pandey Singh holds Rural Development/Rural Works and Panchayati Raj jointly. Jharkhand's Road Safety Lead Agency was constituted within the Department of Transport by Gazette Notification dated 26 March 2017 following a Supreme Court direction, and — because roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List — the Government of Jharkhand's own departments, not the Union Government, are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue in this state; the Union Government matters mainly for National Highway stretches, PMGSY funding rules, and the Motor Vehicles Act's national legal framework.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development & Housing Department (UDHD) and Urban Local Bodies
governance_bodies.mandate: UDHD sets urban policy; its principal implementing arm for infrastructure is JUIDCO (Jharkhand Urban Infrastructure Development Company Limited), incorporated 19 November 2013 under the Companies Act, 1956, as the nodal agency for planning, implementation and management of urban infrastructure projects statewide, including roads, flyovers, drainage, water supply, sewerage and housing. JUIDCO's own site lists concrete road-relevant execution work including the Kanta Toli flyover and the Ratu Road flyover, both in Ranchi.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within Urban Local Bodies (carriageway/footpath); larger urban infrastructure/flyover projects via JUIDCO.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The Jharkhand Municipal Act, 2011 governs all ULBs except cantonments. Jharkhand currently has 48 Urban Local Bodies: 9 Municipal Corporations, 20 Nagar Parishads (Municipal Councils), 19 Nagar Panchayats and 1 Notified Area Committee. By analogy to the Act's general structure, each ULB has an elected head (Mayor/Chairperson/President) and a Deputy, with day-to-day administration under a state-appointed Municipal Commissioner/Executive Officer.

governance_bodies.ranchi_case_study: A single dangerous street in Ranchi can plausibly involve multi-agency overlap, and there is direct, current evidence of exactly this pattern being actively managed at the political level: Ranchi Municipal Corporation (carriageway ownership/maintenance, drainage, street vending organisation) under Mayor Roshini Khalkho and Municipal Commissioner Sushant Gaurav, IAS; RCD/JUIDCO for arterial roads and flyovers (Kanta Toli flyover, Ratu Road flyover); NHAI where a National Highway alignment runs through or bypasses the city (specific current Ranchi-area NHAI projects were not itemised in this pass — a gap to close directly with NHAI's Ranchi/regional office); Jharkhand Police Traffic wing for signal timing, enforcement, diversion management; and RRDA as the plausible town-planning authority (see above). In early September 2026, Chief Minister Hemant Soren personally chaired a joint review of UDHD and RCD specifically to address Ranchi's urban traffic problems — directing officials to identify and close unnecessary median cuts, restrict turns to designated intersections, organise street vending, clear illegal encroachments, and ensure new roads are designed with proper drainage from the planning stage. This is direct, current evidence that fixing an ordinary Ranchi traffic problem in practice requires coordinated action across at least two state departments at the very top of government.

flags.fact: Identity of the current Ranchi Municipal Corporation Deputy Mayor
flags.entity: Ranchi Municipal Corporation
flags.resolution_note: A new internal inconsistency was surfaced in this pass and deliberately NOT resolved one way or the other: following the 2026 municipal election, one source names Sanjeev Vijayvargiya as Deputy Mayor of Ranchi Municipal Corporation, while a different source's leadership listing inconsistently names a 'Neeraj Kumar' as Deputy Mayor instead. Mayor Roshini Khalkho and Municipal Commissioner Sushant Gaurav, IAS are both independently confirmed and not in dispute — only the Deputy Mayor identity is contested. This should be checked directly with the Corporation before citing either name in outreach material; CrashFree India should not treat either name as settled.

flags.fact: Whether 'Transport Commissioner heads Jharkhand's Road Safety Cell/Lead Agency' is a Jharkhand-specific fact or a generically-applied national template
flags.entity: Road Safety Lead Agency / Transport Commissioner (Sanjeev Kumar Besra, IAS)
flags.resolution_note: In most Indian states operating under the SCCoRS framework, the Lead Agency/State Road Safety Cell is headed by the Transport Commissioner. This is confirmed structurally for Jharkhand only to the extent that Jharkhand's own government page confirms a Transport Department Lead Agency exists; the specific 'headed by Transport Commissioner' detail was originally sourced from a road-safety information portal that appears to describe this template generically (and is hosted by an entity associated with Rajasthan), not a Jharkhand-government-specific document. A fresh attempt in this verification pass to find a Jharkhand-specific primary confirmation did not find one. Should be confirmed directly with the Transport Department before being used as a hard fact in outreach material.

flags.fact: Whether Sunil Kumar, IAS holding Principal Secretary of both the Road Construction Department (RCD) and the Urban Development & Housing Department (UDHD) simultaneously is a genuine, sanctioned dual charge
flags.entity: Road Construction Department (RCD) / Urban Development & Housing Department (UDHD) — Principal Secretary post
flags.resolution_note: This pass fetched both departments' current pages independently and found the UDHD page (fetched live) also names Sunil Kumar, IAS as its current Principal Secretary — most likely a genuine, current dual charge (common in Jharkhand IAS administration) rather than an error, upgraded from the prior draft's 'flagged possible error' status. However, this was not confirmed via a third, independent source explicitly stating 'dual charge' — the state file's own Source Audit explicitly treats this as Partially Verified, not fully resolved, even though the changelog lists it under 'Reconfirmed' rather than 'Still Flagged.'
